doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The future of New Orleans music
title: Hopes for New Orleans: Jazz Fest exclusion, Payton and a post-Katrina rebuild
summary: Thanks and best wishes; his group was not hired at Jazz Fest; New Orleans must embrace new ideas as Armstrong and Bechet did; music education was failing before Katrina.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Wow. Well you have told me some fascinating things. It’s been great.
I want to wish you the best of luck with being part of New Orleans coming back, that will be a big thing.

Yeah. Well you know I feel if I’m not a part of it I’ve done my due. I’m 63 years old and I taught for 42 years and I played music for about 45 years so if there’s anything I can do I think I would do it but I taught enough young musicians who are out there that they will be playing for the next 40, 50 years and I had a part to do with that. So if I can do anything I would like New Orleans to open its mind and its ears to other things other than just what it’s been doing. And toward like the end of our gigs at the Jazz Fest, we’ve had full tents, people come looking for us now. But like last year we weren’t hired to play because they figured there wasn’t any room for that particular type of music. Even my group wasn’t hired again. I don’t know. The people in charge of it. There’s no big deal, that’s not my festival. I don’t have to be there. But they would say well your music sounds a certain way, in other words, my music is not valuable enough to bring people or the group with Kidd. We are such a different type of band that we don’t have a place there. And that’s crazy man. Because that’s the way New Orleans music came about. It came about by new ideas. If people like Louis Armstrong and Sidney Bechet and all those early musicians and if they didn’t take it further from the time they were living you’d have never heard of them. So if anything I would like to see New Orleans just open up and embrace the beauty and the things and the people that are there to make it better than it was before. Because there are some young musicians, one of my students, Nicholas Payton, he is really looking into this free expression, avante garde type of thing. He’s done, I mean if you listen to and follow his career and all the records that he has recorded up to this date, he did a sequence of development of music from the beginning, early styles of Louis Armstrong to the modern jazz to the electronic thing and now he’s — so I’m glad to see he’s doing that. I mean you can be comfortable playing like Louis Armstrong and everybody will praise them and bow down, Lord, you know, but he decided that he needs to be truly himself and needs to do something else. Just like Christian Scott. He’s playing the way he wants to play, he’s doing what he wants to do, and he’s getting a lot of play now. So you have to be comfortable with yourself. You have to feel that. And as other people are doing things, as long as they’re comfortable that’s what they want to do that’s cool. That’s for them. It’s cool. So I hope New Orleans can come back, I hope it can be better. There’s a lot of corruption there, man, it’s a lot of jealousy, it’s a lot of small mindedness but man, things are going on and even before © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

Katrina things were going on like in Houston and Atlanta that were flourishing. Even on the Gulf Coast and even with the educational system man. The music thing in New Orleans was suffering even before Katrina. So if we’re going to come back we have to take it from the best part of those years and bring it into something else because our kids deserve that. It hurts when you see kids playing like they’ve never had instructions in their life. And they go to school and they’re taking music classes but they’re not getting the right information, for whatever reason. So I would love to see New Orleans become what it should be, a beautiful place.
